knowledge_point.title: Using the Double-Angle Formula to Simplify Products

question.:question/problem:
Express the following as a constant multiple of a single trigonometric ratio.

$$
\sin^{3}\left(49^\circ\right)\cos\left(49^\circ\right)+\sin\left(49^\circ\right)\cos^{3}\left(49^\circ\right)
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Put $x=49^\circ$. Factor out the common product, then use the Pythagorean identity.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sin^3 x\cos x+\sin x\cos^3 x \\ &=\sin x\cos x(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x) \\ &=\sin x\cos x
\end{aligned}
$$

Recall $2\sin x\cos x=\sin(2x)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin x\cos x &=\frac{1}{2}\left[2\sin x\cos x\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\sin(2x)
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=49^\circ$ and double the whole angle: $2x=98^\circ$. The result is

$$
\frac{1}{2}\sin\left(98^\circ\right) .
$$

question.:question/problem:
Express the following as a constant multiple of a single trigonometric ratio.

$$
-3\sin\left(71^\circ\right)\cos^{3}\left(71^\circ\right)-3\sin^{3}\left(71^\circ\right)\cos\left(71^\circ\right)
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Put $x=71^\circ$. Factor out the common product, then use the Pythagorean identity.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&-3\sin^3 x\cos x-3\sin x\cos^3 x \\ &=-3\sin x\cos x(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x) \\ &=-3\sin x\cos x
\end{aligned}
$$

Recall $2\sin x\cos x=\sin(2x)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
-3\sin x\cos x &=-\frac{3}{2}\left[2\sin x\cos x\right] \\ &=-\frac{3}{2}\sin(2x)
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=71^\circ$ and double the whole angle: $2x=142^\circ$. The result is

$$
-\frac{3}{2}\sin\left(142^\circ\right) .
$$

question.:question/problem:
Express the following as a constant multiple of a single trigonometric ratio.

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\sin^{3}\left(\frac{3\pi}{7}\right)\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{7}\right)-\frac{1}{2}\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{7}\right)\cos^{3}\left(\frac{3\pi}{7}\right)
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Put $x=\frac{3\pi}{7}$. Factor out the common product, then use the Pythagorean identity.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&-\frac{1}{2}\sin^3 x\cos x-\frac{1}{2}\sin x\cos^3 x \\ &=-\frac{1}{2}\sin x\cos x(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x) \\ &=-\frac{1}{2}\sin x\cos x
\end{aligned}
$$

Recall $2\sin x\cos x=\sin(2x)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\frac{1}{2}\sin x\cos x &=-\frac{1}{4}\left[2\sin x\cos x\right] \\ &=-\frac{1}{4}\sin(2x)
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=\frac{3\pi}{7}$ and double the whole angle: $2x=\frac{6\pi}{7}$. The result is

$$
-\frac{1}{4}\sin\left(\frac{6\pi}{7}\right) .
$$

question.:question/problem:
Express the following as a constant multiple of a single trigonometric ratio.

$$
-\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\cos^{3}\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)-\sin^{3}\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{11}\right)
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Put $x=\frac{\pi}{11}$. Factor out the common product, then use the Pythagorean identity.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&-\sin^3 x\cos x-\sin x\cos^3 x \\ &=-\sin x\cos x(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x) \\ &=-\sin x\cos x
\end{aligned}
$$

Recall $2\sin x\cos x=\sin(2x)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\sin x\cos x &=-\frac{1}{2}\left[2\sin x\cos x\right] \\ &=-\frac{1}{2}\sin(2x)
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=\frac{\pi}{11}$ and double the whole angle: $2x=\frac{2\pi}{11}$. The result is

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{11}\right) .
$$
